items.title: Hostile Inference: Exploiting Docker Model Runner for Container Escapes
items.description: Local LLM inference is seeing adoption in default developer workflows, and the tooling that serves those models now ships inside products developers already trust. One of those is Docker Model Runner (DMR), the feature in Docker Desktop that pulls, runs, and serves models locally. In November 2025, we reported ZDI-26-150 / CVE-2026-28400, a denial-of-service (on macOS) stemming from an unauthenticated argument-injection vulnerability in DMR. A container created with the default set of privileges could overwrite and corrupt the Docker Desktop VM’s data disk. Further analysis, under non-default configurations, turned the same primitive into arbitrary code execution on the host, on both macOS and Windows. In this post, we walk through the full chain: the argument-injection primitive, the host file read/write foothold it grants, how we take partial control of what gets written, and the payoff that turns a constrained file write into arbitrary code execution on the host through Docker Extensions. We then cover two further escapes we found along the way: one from an overly permissive Seatbelt sandbox configuration on macOS, and one that pivots the WSL2 VM-to-host boundary through Docker Extensions. Linux containers and the Docker Engine components (runc, containerd, dockerd) run in the Linux VM. items.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
items.description: This seems like a good thing: Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. […] The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. Alternate link. Details: First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Technical paper.

items.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
items.description: Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. items.title: VU#604762: Multiple vendors vulnerable to Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS (APFS)

By supplying an alternative Unicode spelling or case-folded variant (such as ß versus ss) that bypasses the application's file write checks, a local attacker can overwrite files wherever the process has write permissions, potentially leading to data corruption, configuration hijacking, or code execution. Multiple vendors have assigned CVEs and issued patches to address this flaw. Description Several archive tools, packaging systems, and runtimes enforce exclusion filters using pathname comparisons that do not match the underlying filesystem's resolution behavior. ß versus ss), rather than full case folding, a vulnerable application can be tricked into silently overwriting protected files. This vulnerability exposes backup tools, forensic workflows, and CI/CD pipelines to unauthorized file modification. The CVEs assigned during coordination are as follows: CVE-2026-14978 CVE-2026-49401 CVE-2026-45110 CVE-2026-59890 VU#604762.8 Impact Local attackers can bypass file exclusion filters or path locks during archive extraction to overwrite files anywhere the process has write permissions, potentially leading to data corruption, configuration hijacking, or code execution. This risk extends to supply chain workflows, where the failure to correctly exclude items can result in the inadvertent inclusion of sensitive files in distributed artifacts or the corruption of CI/CD build steps. items.title: Usable Security at Luxury Hotels
items.description: Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved. This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. Even worse, in this case the guest-first culture punishes hesitation. More interesting, the case study shows that splitting security between owner, operator, and brand leaves nobody accountable. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.
